frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND LOGISTICS CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability, rail failures, and congested ports continue to limit South Africa's ability to process and export resources on sovereign terms. Public-private reforms are advancing but remain vulnerable to regulatory and political friction.

frictionVectors.title: MINERALS INVESTMENT COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, and European partners are competing for access to platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic minerals. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while avoiding excessive dependence on any single external bloc.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE ON SUDAN
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports remain dependent on infrastructure crossing war-torn Sudan, exposing revenue flows to conflict damage, political leverage, and opaque transit arrangements. Production and public finances remain highly vulnerable to interruptions.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL CONTROL OF OIL OPERATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and regional intermediaries retain substantial influence over production, financing, and export logistics. Weak institutions and elite competition limit the state's ability to convert oil wealth into broad-based development.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD SMUGGLING AND EXTERNAL PATRONAGE
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and commercial networks use gold to finance the war, with regional and international buyers benefiting from weak oversight. This sustains conflict while depriving the formal state of revenue.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND PIPELINE DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Fighting threatens transport corridors, refineries, and export infrastructure around the Red Sea and central Sudan. External powers retain leverage through arms, diplomatic support, and access to strategic maritime and mineral assets.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and corridor projects are drawing competing interest from Gulf, Chinese, Indian, and Western investors. Dar es Salaam is gaining strategic importance, but financing terms and operational control remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: MINING AND LNG BARGAINING
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater local value capture from gold, critical minerals, and planned LNG while trying to preserve investor confidence. Contract transparency, environmental concerns, and local-content demands remain recurring sources of friction.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is central to Togo's trade and regional influence, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign capital, operators, and security partnerships. Disruptions in the Gulf of Guinea or the Sahel could quickly affect revenue and supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate production remains strategically important, yet limited downstream processing constrains sovereign value capture. State control is balanced against external financing needs and competition from larger regional producers.

highlights: Phosphate and gas sector under fiscal strain

frictionVectors.title: European Union conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia relies heavily on European trade, financing, and energy partnerships, giving Brussels significant leverage over migration cooperation and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import dependence
frictionVectors.details: High reliance on imported hydrocarbons and limited domestic investment constrain Tunisian control over energy security and expose the country to external price shocks.

highlights: Oil development tied to regional corridors

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to national resource ambitions but faces international criticism, financing constraints, and environmental opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects expand infrastructure capacity while increasing exposure to external lenders and repayment pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic processing and revenue capture, but foreign firms still dominate major mining assets, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Western-backed and Chinese-linked transport options are competing to shape Zambia's mineral export routes, giving infrastructure partners strategic influence over copper access.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain prominent in lithium, platinum, and gold, while Zimbabwe seeks tighter beneficiation rules and stronger state revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Financial isolation and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted market access, and chronic currency instability push Harare toward alternative financiers and barter-style resource arrangements, reducing bargaining flexibility.
